claim: A chemist's spilled powder tasted bitter to his colleague and of nothing to him.

start.title: Taste
start.description: Sense of chemicals on the tongue

end.title: TAS2R38
end.description: Protein-coding gene in the species Homo sapiens

knots.passage: Researchers use two synthetic substances, phenylthiocarbamide (PTC) and 6-n-propylthiouracil (PROP) to study the genetics of bitter perception. These two substances taste bitter to some people, but are virtually tasteless to others.
knots.hatnote: Some bitter chemicals don't taste bitter to everyone.

knots.passage: The tested genetic taste phenomenon of PTC was discovered in 1931 when DuPont chemist Arthur Fox accidentally released a cloud of fine crystalline PTC. A nearby colleague complained about the bitter taste, while Fox, who was closer and should have received a strong dose, tasted nothing. Fox then continued to test the taste buds of assorted family and friends, setting the groundwork for future genetic studies. The genetic penetrance was so strong that it was used in paternity tests before the advent of DNA matching.
knots.hatnote: The discovery was a lab accident.

knots.passage: Chimpanzees and orangutans also vary in their ability to taste PTC, with the proportions of tasters and non-tasters similar to that in humans. The ability to taste PTC is an ancestral trait of hominids that has been independently lost in humans and chimpanzees, through distinct mutations at TAS2R38.
knots.hatnote: Humans are not the only ones split into tasters and non-tasters.

knots.passage: As with watercress, mustard greens, turnip, broccoli and horseradish, human perception of bitterness in rutabaga is governed by a gene affecting the TAS2R bitter receptor, which detects the glucosinolates in rutabaga. Sensitive individuals with the genotype PAV/PAV (supertasters) find rutabaga twice as bitter as insensitive subjects (AVI/AVI). The difference for the mixed type (PAV/AVI) is insignificant for rutabaga. As a result, sensitive individuals may find some rutabagas too bitter to eat.
knots.hatnote: The same gene decides how your vegetables taste.

knots.passage: Bitter taste receptors exhibit expression in various cell types within the sinonasal and airway regions. Other ligands that activate T2R38 are N-Acyl homoserine lactones (AHLs) are a class of signaling molecules involved in bacterial quorum sensing. Upon encountering these agonists, the receptors initiate a signaling cascade that relies on T2R activation. Consequently, this cascade triggers the release of nitric oxide (NO), a potent bactericidal agent, thereby promoting both bactericidal activity and an enhancement in mucociliary clearance (MCC).
knots.hatnote: But this 'taste' receptor also turns up far from the tongue.

payoff: One puff of spilled powder exposed a gene that makes rutabaga taste twice as bitter to some, and helps the nose fight bacteria.
